chapters.title: Chapter 4: India's Position in the New Trade Order

lessons.title: India as a China+1 Beneficiary: PLI Schemes, Electronics and Pharma Exports

children.text: India's two biggest China+1 success stories look almost nothing alike. Electronics manufacturing is a new industry, built from a near-standing start over roughly a decade, riding a wave of deliberate corporate diversification away from a single country. Pharmaceutical exports are the opposite: a decades-old, already-dominant global industry that recent policy has reinforced rather than created. Understanding why they took such different paths tells you far more about how to judge India's next sectoral bet than simply reading both as "PLI worked here."

body.text: Electronics PLI built a new export industry almost from zero. Pharma PLI is de-risking an industry that was already the world's largest generics supplier. Both count as China+1 wins, but only one of them is actually a story about creating new capacity.

children.text: Electronics: From Assembly Line to Export Line

India's electronics exports have grown roughly fivefold over a decade, from around $6 billion in FY15 to roughly $29 billion by FY24. Mobile phones did most of the heavy lifting: phone exports rose from a little over $1.5 billion in FY18 to more than $15 billion by FY24, with Apple's assembly partners, Foxconn, Pegatron and, since Tata Group's 2023 acquisition of Wistron's Karnataka plant, Tata Electronics itself, accounting for the largest share of that growth.

body.title: India's Mobile Phone Exports, FY18-FY24 (Illustrative, USD Billion)

body.text: Export value is not the same as domestic value capture. Domestic value addition in Indian phone assembly is still commonly estimated in the 15% to 20% range for many models, since displays, chips and other high-value components largely arrive imported, mostly the component ecosystem gap Chapter 3 already flagged for India specifically. A rising export number and a rising share of India-made value are two different claims, and only the first one is clearly true yet.

children.text: Pharma: Reinforcing an Industry That Was Already Dominant

India's pharmaceutical export strength was not built by PLI at all. It was built over three decades, starting when companies like Ranbaxy, Dr Reddy's, Cipla and Sun Pharma began systematically filing Abbreviated New Drug Applications with the US FDA from the 1990s onward, turning India into what the industry calls the "pharmacy of the world." By the time PLI schemes arrived in 2020, India was already supplying an estimated 20% of the world's generic medicines by volume and roughly 60% of the world's vaccine doses by volume, led by the Serum Institute of India, the world's largest vaccine manufacturer.

So what was PLI actually for here? Chapter 1 already showed the answer: the 2020 COVID shock exposed that roughly two-thirds of India's active pharmaceutical ingredient needs came from a single country, China. A dedicated API PLI scheme, launched in 2020 with an outlay of roughly ₹6,940 crore, targets 41 critical bulk drugs and key starting materials specifically, funding new domestic manufacturing capacity through bulk drug parks. A separate, larger PLI scheme for pharmaceuticals, with an outlay of roughly ₹15,000 crore, targets higher-value complex generics, biosimilars and in-vitro diagnostics, aiming to move India's export mix upmarket rather than simply defending its existing generics volume.

body.title: Two China+1 Stories, Two Different Mechanisms

columns.label: Electronics
points: Built new export capacity from a near-zero base
Driven by customer diversification, especially Apple's supply chain strategy
PLI is the primary reason this capacity exists at all
Domestic value addition remains a genuine, unresolved weakness

columns.label: Pharma
points: Reinforces a dominant industry built over three decades
Driven by an existing global cost and regulatory advantage
PLI targets a specific vulnerability, API import dependence, not the whole industry
Domestic value addition is already high; the goal is upstream security, not new market entry

body.title: Test the distinction
body.question: Which statement most accurately distinguishes India's electronics PLI story from its pharma PLI story?
options: Electronics PLI failed while pharma PLI succeeded
Electronics PLI created a new export industry largely from scratch, while pharma PLI reinforced an already-dominant industry against a specific vulnerability
Both PLI programmes target the same underlying goal, growing export volume
Pharma PLI is larger in total outlay than every other PLI sector combined
body.explanation: Electronics PLI built genuinely new capacity and export volume from a small base. Pharma's export dominance long predates PLI, so its PLI schemes are targeted at a specific weakness, API import dependence, and at moving up the value chain, not at creating the underlying industry.

body.title: Size the export growth
body.prompt: India's mobile phone exports rose from approximately $1.6 billion in FY18 to approximately $15.6 billion in FY24. Approximately how many times larger were FY24 exports compared to FY18, rounded to the nearest whole number?
body.explanation: $15.6 billion divided by $1.6 billion is approximately 9.75, which rounds to about 10 times. That is an unusually fast scale-up for any export category over six years, and it happened almost entirely within the PLI policy window.

cards.definition: The share of a finished product's value that is actually created within the country, as opposed to imported as components or sub-assemblies; a key gap in India's electronics manufacturing story.
India's long-standing informal title as the world's largest supplier of generic medicines by volume, built through decades of FDA-compliant manufacturing and ANDA filings.
A 2020 Production Linked Incentive scheme, outlay roughly ₹6,940 crore, targeting 41 critical bulk drugs and key starting materials to reduce India's import dependence, mainly on China.

points: India's electronics exports grew roughly fivefold from FY15 to FY24, with mobile phones, led by Apple's assembly partners, driving most of that growth almost entirely within the PLI policy window.
Domestic value addition in Indian phone assembly remains commonly estimated in the 15% to 20% range, a live weakness tied to the component ecosystem gap raised in Chapter 3.
India's pharma export dominance, roughly 20% of global generic medicine volume and roughly 60% of global vaccine doses, was built over three decades, well before PLI existed.
Pharma PLI targets a specific vulnerability, API import dependence on China, exposed sharply by the 2020 COVID shock, rather than creating the underlying export industry.
The same policy tool, PLI, is doing genuinely different jobs in these two sectors: creating new capacity in electronics, and de-risking an already-dominant supply chain in pharma.
When evaluating any new PLI sector going forward, ask which of these two patterns it resembles, since the realistic timeline and risk profile for each is very different.
